Q: Volumes on Docker Compose A:

New response

Having reproduced your set-up, this precise error message happens when I intentionally comment out the top-level volumes section:

#volumes:

#  nuc_docker:
#    name: node-red_docker
#    external: true

service "node-red" refers to undefined volume nuc13_docker: invalid compose project

Therefore, I clearly suspect an invisible or invalid character, probably in the first volume name (nut_docker).

Delete completely the top-level volumes section and rewrite it by hand (avoid copy-paste).

Initial (off-topic) response

According to the Compose reference, the external: true attribute indicates the volume is managed outside of this Compose file.

Either you have another Compose file that declares this volume (in the case, you have to docker compose up -d it first), or you have to manually create the external volume first (docker volume create node-red_docker).

Q: Spring Boot not loading environment variables from .env file in application.properties A:

Spring Boot can resolve OS environment variables automatically, but it does not treat a .env file as “environment variables” the way Node/Ruby do. Spring only sees what’s in the Spring Environment (config files + real env vars + system props, etc.).

Is spring.config.import enough?

Yes, it can be — if your .env is loaded as a properties file and Spring actually finds it at runtime.

Your .env content (KEY=value) is already “.properties-like”, so this is valid in principle (many people do exactly this).

The two most common reasons it still fails:

  1. The file isn’t being found because file: paths are resolved relative to the process working directory, which differs between:

  • IntelliJ/VS Code run config

  • mvn spring-boot:run

  • running a fat jar from another directory

  1. The file isn’t being treated as a properties file (naming/extension or import syntax issues).

I propose 2 options for your use case

Option 1 — Keep .env, but import it explicitly and safely

--> in your application.properties

spring.config.import=optional:file:./.env[.properties]

spring.datasource.url=${DB_URL}
spring.datasource.username=${POSTGRESQL}
spring.datasource.password=${PASSWORD}

--> in your .env (must be plain key=value, no export, no quotes needed)

DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:3005/01blog
POSTGRESQL=postgres
PASSWORD=f

Key point: file:./.env means “look in the working directory”. So in your IDE, set Working directory to the project root (or wherever .env is). If you run the jar from another folder, it won’t find the file.

If you want to avoid “working directory” issues entirely, import with an absolute path (or a path relative to something stable like ${user.home}).

Option 2 — Don’t use .env; use real environment variables (most “Spring-native”)

Spring Boot already supports OS environment variables with high precedence.

So you can simply set:

  • DB_URL

  • POSTGRESQL

  • PASSWORD

in your IDE Run Configuration, shell, Docker, Kubernetes, etc., and keep:

spring.datasource.url=${DB_URL}
spring.datasource.username=${POSTGRESQL}
spring.datasource.password=${PASSWORD}

In my opinion, i recommand you the second option, this is the most portable approach for production.

Hope this will help :)
